He even practised his bow in the corridor. Then he walks on stage, opens his mouth, and forgets his first line. Completely. Silence. And for one second, Vikas, I felt this hot little jolt of joy. Like, yes. Finally. I actually had to press my lips together. Then he looked at the teachers, his ears went red, and he said "sorry" in this tiny voice, and I felt sick at myself. He's annoying, but he's not a villain. I've forgotten lines too. So I don't know what I am. Happy? Ashamed? Both, I think. I haven't told anyone except you.

passage: I'm Ojas, Harish's classmate. On Friday the district band results went up on the music-room door. Neel, who'd spent a month telling everyone he was a "sure thing" on drums, wasn't on the list. Harish was standing next to me. I saw it: a quick grin, a squeezed fist, like he'd scored a goal. Harish lost the drum spot to Neel last year, and Neel never let him forget it. But then Neel came round the corner, read the list, and just walked off with his hands in his pockets. Harish's grin went. He stared at the floor for a while. On the bus he was quiet, and I saw him type something to Neel. I don't know what it said, or whether he felt guilty or just awkward. But he didn't join the jokes at the back of the bus.

qa.q: Where did the district band results go up?
qa.a: On the music-room door.

qa.q: What does Harish's grin fading and his stare at the floor suggest?
qa.a: After a flash of pleasure at his rival's failure, he seemed uneasy, perhaps guilty, once he saw Neel walk off hurt.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make on the bus, and why does it stand out?
qa.a: He stayed out of the jokes at the back and typed something to Neel, choosing not to pile onto Neel's fall.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt reading the list?
qa.a: Neel had called himself a "sure thing", so missing out in front of everyone probably felt crushing and embarrassing; he walked off with his hands in his pockets.

passage: Tuesday. Wasim struts into the canteen. "Solo's mine. The judges already love me." Suraj stirs his dal and says nothing, jaw tight. He has been practising the same song for a month. Thursday. Audition day. Wasim's voice cracks on the high note, twice. Someone laughs. Suraj feels a quick bright spark of glee, a little voice saying serves him right. Then he sees Wasim's hands shaking on the mic stand, and the spark turns sour in his stomach. Suraj sings next and does fine. Monday. The list is out: Suraj has the solo. Wasim passes him in the corridor, not boasting now. Suraj stops him. "Your first verse was really good, you know. The note just got you." Wasim blinks. "Thanks." Suraj walks on, lighter, and still a bit ashamed of Thursday's spark.

passage:
Aadhya, you're sulking because Riya got the solo, na? Sit. Let your Ira Maasi tell you something I've never told anyone.
When I was fifteen, there was a girl in my dance class called Pushpalata. Every week she told us the lead in the Republic Day dance was hers. "Madam already decided," she'd say, fixing her bun. At the audition, in front of the whole school, she spun, slipped and landed flat on the stage. And I felt it: a hot little jump of joy. Like, good, finally.
Then I saw her face. She was trying so hard not to cry. And my joy turned sour in my stomach. I went home ashamed. I'd wanted the lead too, and I'd let that make me glad someone got hurt.
I never said sorry, because I never said anything. I still wish I'd helped her up.

qa.q: What happened to Pushpalata at the audition?
qa.a: She spun, slipped and landed flat on the stage.

qa.q: Why did young Ira's joy turn sour in her stomach?
qa.a: Seeing Pushpalata trying not to cry made her ashamed that her own envy had made her glad someone got hurt.

qa.q: What choice does Ira Maasi wish she had made at that moment?
qa.a: She wishes she had helped Pushpalata up, turning the flash of glee into kindness instead of silent shame.

qa.q: What might Pushpalata have felt, falling after weeks of boasting?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated and exposed, fighting tears in front of the whole school.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage flash of joy at a boastful rival's fall at an audition, followed by shame.

passage: The bus from Thane broke down, so Kiran reached the youth theatre audition soaked, with ten minutes to spare. In the lobby, Salma was already talking loudly. "Honestly, the director called me last week. The part's mine." Kiran, sixteen, squeezed water from his sleeves and said nothing. He'd wanted that part for a year. At four the list went up. Salma's name wasn't on it. For a second, Kiran felt a bright jolt of delight, like winning a bet. Then Salma walked out past him, chin up, eyes wet, into the rain without an umbrella. The feeling in his chest twisted into something heavy. He looked down at his own dripping shoes. Then he ran after her and held out his umbrella. "Take it. I'm already wet."

qa.q: How did Kiran arrive at the audition?
qa.a: Soaked, with ten minutes to spare, after the bus from Thane broke down.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's delight twist into something heavy?
qa.a: Seeing Salma walk out with wet eyes made him ashamed of feeling glad; his envy and his sense of fairness pulled against each other.

qa.q: What turning point did Kiran choose, and what did it change?
qa.a: He ran after Salma with his umbrella, acting on his kinder feeling instead of the flash of glee.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when Kiran offers his umbrella?
qa.a: She might be surprised and touched, perhaps embarrassed too, since she boasted to him earlier.

grounding: A teen feels a flash of joy at a boastful rival's failed audition, then shame, and offers help.
